title: Circuit breakers, bulkheads, rate limiters and graceful degradation
seriesDescription: Topic-by-topic JEE-style quizzes for the backend and AI-engineering interview roadmap: integer, assertion-reason, matrix match, fill-in-the-blanks, short code writing, plus multi-correct questions. Language core, concurrency, DSA, web frameworks, data access, databases, messaging, resilience, security, testing, system design, LLM and agent engineering.
description: The circuit-breaker state machine, token-bucket arithmetic, bulkhead sizing, Resilience4j / pybreaker / slowapi usage, and designing safe fallbacks.
source: Resilience4j documentation; Martin Fowler on circuit breakers; Release It! (Nygard); pybreaker and slowapi docs; Stripe engineering blog on rate limiters; Google SRE book (handling overload)

questions.prompt: Match each circuit-breaker state with its behaviour.

right.text: Calls pass through and failures are counted
Calls are rejected immediately without contacting the dependency
A limited number of trial calls decide whether to close or reopen
Calls are queued until the dependency recovers

questions.explanation: CLOSED to OPEN when the failure (or slow-call) rate crosses the threshold; OPEN to HALF_OPEN after the wait duration; HALF_OPEN to CLOSED if trial calls succeed, else back to OPEN.

questions.prompt: Resilience4j count-based breaker: slidingWindowSize = 10, minimumNumberOfCalls = 10, failureRateThreshold = 50 (percent). After 10 calls, what is the smallest number of failed calls that opens the circuit?
questions.explanation: The breaker opens when the failure rate is greater than or equal to the threshold: 5 of 10 is 50 percent. Fewer than minimumNumberOfCalls never opens it.

questions.prompt: A token bucket has capacity 10 and refills 2 tokens per second, and starts full. At t = 0 ten requests arrive and are all served. At t = 4 s, nine requests arrive at once. How many are served?
questions.explanation: The bucket was empty at t = 0 and refills 2 x 4 = 8 tokens by t = 4 (below the cap of 10), so 8 of the 9 are served and 1 is rejected.

questions.prompt: A bulkhead allows at most 10 concurrent calls to a dependency and each call takes 200 ms. By Little's law, what is the maximum throughput to that dependency in requests per second?
questions.explanation: Throughput = concurrency / latency = 10 / 0.2 = 50 per second. If latency rises to 1 s, the same bulkhead only allows 10 per second, which is the protective point.

questions.prompt: Match each rate-limiting algorithm with its characteristic.

right.text: Allows bursts up to the bucket size, then a steady refill rate
Smooths traffic to a constant outflow rate
Cheap but a client can send double the limit across a window boundary
Stores a timestamp per request, exact but memory heavy
Blocks every request after the first failure

questions.explanation: Fixed-window boundary burst: with 100 per minute, 100 requests at 0:59 and 100 at 1:01 make 200 in two seconds. Sliding window counters approximate the log cheaply.

questions.prompt: Annotate getStock(String sku) so calls go through a Resilience4j circuit breaker named "inventory" and fall back to a method named stockFallback when the call fails or the circuit is open.
questions.model:
@CircuitBreaker(name = "inventory", fallbackMethod = "stockFallback")
public Stock getStock(String sku) { return client.fetch(sku); }
questions.explanation: The fallback must be in the same class with the same parameters plus an optional exception argument, e.g. stockFallback(String sku, Throwable t). Calls must cross the Spring proxy, so self-invocation does not trigger the breaker.

questions.prompt: Write the application.yml for a Resilience4j circuit breaker instance named inventory with a sliding window of 10 calls, a 50 percent failure-rate threshold, and 30 seconds in the open state before half-open.
questions.model:
resilience4j:
  circuitbreaker:
    instances:
      inventory:
        slidingWindowSize: 10
        failureRateThreshold: 50
        waitDurationInOpenState: 30s
questions.explanation: Spring Boot relaxed binding accepts both camelCase and kebab-case keys. Add permittedNumberOfCallsInHalfOpenState and slowCallDurationThreshold to also trip on latency.

questions.prompt: With pybreaker, create a breaker named breaker that opens after 5 consecutive failures and tries again after 30 seconds, then decorate call_api with it.
questions.explanation: When open, pybreaker raises CircuitBreakerError immediately. Catch it to run a fallback. For asyncio code use breaker.call_async or an async-aware library, because the plain decorator is for sync functions.

questions.prompt: In a FastAPI app using slowapi, limiter is already created. Rate limit the route handler search to 5 requests per minute per client, with the handler taking the request argument slowapi requires.
questions.explanation: slowapi needs the Request parameter to read the client key (for example get_remote_address). Register app.state.limiter and the RateLimitExceeded handler. Behind a proxy use the forwarded address, and use Redis storage when running several workers.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion A and the reason R, then choose the correct relationship between them.
questions.assertion: A circuit breaker protects both the caller and a struggling dependency.
questions.reason: While the circuit is open, calls fail immediately instead of consuming caller threads and adding load to the dependency.

whys.a: Correct: fail-fast saves caller resources and gives the dependency room to recover.
whys.b: R is the mechanism, so it explains A.

questions.explanation: Pair the breaker with timeouts; without timeouts a breaker never sees a failure from a hung call.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion A and the reason R, then choose the correct relationship between them.
questions.assertion: A token bucket permits a short burst of requests up to its capacity.
questions.reason: A leaky bucket sends requests to the backend at a constant rate.

whys.a: Leaky bucket behaviour does not explain the token bucket burst.
whys.b: Correct: both are true but describe two different algorithms; the burst comes from stored tokens.

questions.explanation: Token bucket: bursty but bounded average. Leaky bucket: smooth output, queued excess. Stripe uses token buckets for request limiting.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion A and the reason R, then choose the correct relationship between them.
questions.assertion: Rate limiting by API key rather than with one global limit stops a single noisy tenant from starving the others.
questions.reason: A single global limit treats every client separately, so it protects each of them equally.

whys.a: R is false so it cannot explain A.
whys.c: Correct: per-key limits isolate tenants (A true); a global limit pools them all (R false).

questions.explanation: Use layered limits: per key, per IP, per endpoint, plus a global safety limit and load shedding.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion A and the reason R, then choose the correct relationship between them.
questions.assertion: In the HALF_OPEN state a circuit breaker lets all traffic through to test whether the dependency has recovered.
questions.reason: HALF_OPEN permits only a configured number of trial calls and decides to close or reopen from their results.

whys.d: Correct: only a few probe calls are allowed (R true), so A is false.

questions.explanation: Letting everyone through at once could knock the recovering service over again.

questions.text: When a dependency fails, return a {1} such as cached data, hide non-critical {2} behind flags, and use load {3} to drop low-priority requests under overload.
questions.explanation: Degrade in layers from stale data to reduced features to explicit errors, and tell the client when data is stale.

questions.prompt: Which are sound degradation strategies when a dependency is down? Select all that apply.

options.text: Serve the last known recommendations from cache and mark them stale.
options.why: Right: a slightly stale list beats an error page for non-critical content.

options.text: Hide the reviews widget while the reviews service is unavailable.
options.why: Right: the core purchase flow keeps working without it.

options.text: Queue the confirmation email and send it when the mail service returns.
options.why: Right: deferring non-urgent work avoids failing the whole order.

options.text: Report a payment as successful when the gateway cannot be reached.
options.why: This invents a financial outcome and creates unrecoverable inconsistency.

options.text: Return an empty 200 for a failed balance lookup, with no signal.
options.why: Silent wrong data is worse than an honest error for a critical read.

questions.explanation: A good fallback is honest, safe for the business, and observable (metric and log every fallback so you notice).

questions.prompt: With the default Resilience4j Spring Boot aspect ordering, which decorator is the outermost one wrapping the others?

options.why: Right: the order is Retry ( CircuitBreaker ( RateLimiter ( TimeLimiter ( Bulkhead ( function ) ) ) ) ).
Bulkhead is the innermost, closest to your function.
CircuitBreaker sits inside Retry so each attempt is recorded by the breaker.
TimeLimiter is inside RateLimiter and CircuitBreaker, nearer the function.

questions.explanation: Retry outside the breaker means each retry attempt is seen (and may be rejected) by the breaker. You can change the order with the aspect-order properties.
